name: awk
one_line: Treat each line as fields and run a tiny program: print columns, filter, count, add up.
plain: Treat each line as fields and run a tiny program: print columns, filter, count, add up.
The sections below show when to use it, real examples, and the options explained in plain English.
when: Pull a column out of a log, `/etc/passwd`, `ps` or a CSV.
Count events per IP or user (a one-line report).
Sum or average numbers; reformat output.

examples.title: Count per IP (associative array)
examples.cmd: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) print c[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn

examples.title: Sum a column
examples.cmd: awk '{s += $NF} END {print s, "bytes in", NR, "requests"}' access.log

examples.title: Format a small report
examples.output:
USER         UID   
root         0     
alice        1001  
bob          1002  
svc-backup   998

mistakes: Single-quote the program; double quotes let the shell expand `$1` first.
Fields are 1-based; `$0` is the whole line.
Quoted strings inside awk use double quotes; escape them inside `bash -c`.
awk is not one program: gawk (used for these examples), mawk (the default on some Ubuntu installs) and BSD awk differ in features such as `asort`, `--version` and regex intervals.
try: Print the unique status codes in `access.log` with counts.
Print lines where the byte count is greater than 1000.
Print each username in `users.txt` in upper case (`toupper`).
